Cancer risk factors

The risk factor categories

Mechanism first

Carcinogens damage DNA, and cells that skip apoptosis and the immune system's checks keep dividing. One exposure rarely does it; exposures and mutations add up over a lifetime.

Priority actions
  • Sort every risk into modifiable (lifestyle, diet, smoking, alcohol) or nonmodifiable (age, genetics).
  • Look for hereditary red flags and refer for genetic counseling when they appear.
Patient example

A client has a sister and a mother with breast and ovarian cancer and was herself diagnosed at 38. That is a younger-than-usual age plus two first-degree relatives, so a BRCA mutation is suspected.

Common trap

Do not call a genetic syndrome the main cause of cancer. It accounts for only 5 to 10%.

Memory trick

Nine boxes to fill: C-E-H-G-L-I-M-I-N (carcinogens, environment, hormones, genetics, lifestyle, infectious disease, medications, immune status, nutrition).

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The most common risk factor is exposure to a .
  • Known genetic syndromes account for of cancers.
  • also raises the risk of pancreatic and prostate cancer and melanoma.
Key ideas
  • The nine risk factor categories are carcinogens, environment, hormones, genetics, lifestyle, infectious disease, medications, immune status and nutrition.
  • Carcinogen exposure is the most common risk factor, and risks are cumulative.
  • Age and genetics cannot be changed; 5 to 10% of cancers come from known genetic syndromes such as BRCA1/2.
  • Hereditary red flags are multiple primaries, bilateral tumors in paired organs, a younger-than-usual age, a tumor in the sex not usually affected, and two or more first-degree relatives with the same cancer.
  • BRCA2 also raises the risk of pancreatic and prostate cancer and melanoma.
Source: study guide, Ch 13

Risk factors by cancer (Table 13.2)

Mechanism first

Each cancer has its own typical exposure, and the table pairs them. Look at what damages the organ: tobacco the lung, hepatitis the liver, H. pylori the stomach, HPV the cervix.

Priority actions
  • When a history gives a risk set, name the cancer it points to.
  • Teach the client how to change the modifiable factors in that set.
Patient example

A client with an undescended testicle in childhood now has a painless scrotal lump. The risk set points to testicular cancer.

Common trap

Do not mix risk sets between cancers: unopposed estrogen is uterine, not cervical; HPV is cervical, not uterine.

Memory trick

Pair the organ with its culprit: stomach-H. pylori, liver-hepatitis, cervix-HPV, testis-undescended.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The greatest risk for testicular cancer is .
  • Cervical cancer is tied to .
  • Liver cancer is tied to alcohol and hepatitis .
Key ideas
  • Cervical cancer: HPV, multiple partners, early sexual contact, tobacco use.
  • Gastric cancer: H. pylori, alcohol, ulcers, smoking. Liver cancer: alcohol and hepatitis A, B or C.
  • Testicular cancer: undescended testicle is the greatest risk. Lung cancer: tobacco, asbestos, coal, soot, tar, pollution, wood dust.
  • Uterine cancer: estrogen therapy without progesterone, obesity, tamoxifen, PCOS, diabetes.
Source: study guide, Ch 13 Table 13.2

Levels of prevention

Mechanism first

Prevention works at three points on the timeline: before the cancer starts, while it is small, and after diagnosis.

Priority actions
  • Primary: vaccinate, remove carcinogens, change lifestyle.
  • Secondary: screen on schedule.
  • Tertiary: manage side effects and complications.
Patient example

Giving the HPV vaccine is primary prevention. Booking a colonoscopy at 45 is secondary prevention. Managing nausea during chemotherapy is tertiary.

Common trap

Screening does not prevent the cancer; it finds it early. That makes it secondary prevention.

Memory trick

1-2-3: Prevent, Find, Limit harm.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Immunization is prevention.
  • Screening is prevention.
  • Reducing harm after diagnosis is prevention.
Key ideas
  • Primary prevention: risk factor modification, immunization (HPV, hepatitis), chemoprevention and avoiding carcinogens.
  • Secondary prevention: screening for early detection (breast, cervical, colon, prostate).
  • Tertiary prevention: reducing morbidity and mortality once disease is diagnosed.
Source: study guide, Ch 13 and class notes

CAUTION warning signs

Mechanism first

Early cancer often shows as a small change that persists. The CAUTION list names the seven changes that should not be ignored.

Priority actions
  • Ask about each CAUTION sign.
  • Send any sign that lasts more than 2 weeks for evaluation.
Patient example

A client mentions a mole that has changed in color and a cough that will not go away for 3 weeks. Both are CAUTION signs lasting past 2 weeks.

Common trap

A sign that is mild still counts; the 2-week mark is what triggers evaluation.

Memory trick

CAUTION: Change, A sore, Unusual bleeding, Thickening, Indigestion, Obvious wart or mole change, Nagging cough.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • A sign lasting more than needs evaluation.
  • The N stands for .
  • The A stands for a .
Key ideas
  • C change in bowel or bladder habits; A a sore that does not heal; U unusual bleeding or discharge; T thickening or lump.
  • I indigestion or difficulty swallowing; O obvious change in a wart or mole; N nagging cough or hoarseness.
  • A sign lasting more than 2 weeks needs evaluation.
Source: study guide, Ch 13

Cancer staging (TNM, sizes)

TNM, stages and grade

Mechanism first

Staging asks how big and how far; grading asks how abnormal the cells look. T, N and M are the three questions that decide the stage.

Priority actions
  • Read the TNM letters first; M1 always means spread.
  • Correct teaching when a client calls a stage III or M1 tumor local.
Patient example

A client with T3, N2, M1 breast cancer says she is relieved it is still local. The M1 says otherwise, so she needs more teaching.

Common trap

Do not mix grade and stage. Grade is differentiation; stage is spread.

Memory trick

T = Tumor size, N = Nodes, M = Mets.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • M1 means .
  • All hematologic malignancies are stage at diagnosis.
  • Poorly differentiated cells are .
Key ideas
  • T is the size of the tumor, N is the number of lymph nodes involved, and M is the presence of metastasis; M1 means the cancer is not local.
  • Stage I is small with no obvious spread outside the organ, stage II invades deeper tissue or local nodes, stage III is large or locally advanced, and stage IV has metastasized.
  • All hematologic malignancies are stage IV at diagnosis.
  • Grade describes how differentiated the cells are; poorly differentiated cells are more aggressive.
Source: study guide, Ch 13 and class PLQ

Size and stage tables

Mechanism first

Each organ has its own size and spread cutoffs. Memorize the breakpoints that change a stage.

Priority actions
  • Place a tumor by size first, then nodes, then metastasis.
  • Know that Gleason is a grade of the cells, not a stage.
Patient example

A 3.5 cm breast tumor with no nodes and no metastasis falls in the 2 to 5 cm band with no nodes, which is stage IIA.

Common trap

Do not read Gleason 9 as stage 9. Gleason has a maximum of 10 and is a grade.

Memory trick

Breast cutoffs: 2, 5, then node counts 4, 9, 10.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Breast stage I is a tumor of .
  • Prostate T2 is .
  • The maximum Gleason score is .
Key ideas
  • Breast sizes: 2 cm or less is stage I, 2 to 5 cm is stage II, over 5 cm is stage IIB or III; nodes 4 to 8 is IIIA, up to 9 is IIIB, 10 or more is IIIC.
  • Prostate: T1 cannot be felt, T2 is confined to the prostate, T3 is locally extensive, T4 invades neighboring organs.
  • Gleason is two grades of 1 to 5 added together, maximum 10; higher is worse.
  • Ovarian FIGO: I ovaries, II pelvis, III peritoneum and/or nodes, IV distant.
Source: study guide, Ch 65 and Ch 66

Biopsy procedures

Biopsy types and what they prove

Mechanism first

Only tissue shows what the cells are, so only a biopsy can prove cancer. Imaging and labs point; the biopsy proves.

Priority actions
  • Prepare the client for the type of biopsy.
  • Explain that results take 3 to 10 days.
Patient example

A CT shows a breast mass. The nurse explains the excisional biopsy is preferred because it removes the whole mass with a margin.

Common trap

Do not choose PSA, CT or a tumor marker as the diagnostic test; they only support the diagnosis.

Memory trick

Excisional = take it all out. Incisional = cuts in (and can seed cells).

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The most specific diagnostic test is a .
  • Results take .
  • A negative sentinel node means no further nodes are .
Key ideas
  • A biopsy is the most specific test and is required for a definite diagnosis; labs and imaging are supportive; results take 3 to 10 days.
  • Excisional biopsy removes the whole mass with a margin and is preferred; incisional (core) biopsy can track cells through normal tissue.
  • Fine-needle aspiration is less traumatic but gives fewer cells; core needle gives a larger sample; vacuum-assisted uses a probe with no sutures.
  • A negative sentinel node means no further nodes are removed; a positive one leads to an axillary dissection of 20 to 40 nodes.
  • A liquid biopsy is a blood test for cancer cells or tumor DNA.
Source: study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 65

Biopsy by site

Mechanism first

Each organ has its own best sampling method, and in one place (the ovary) sampling is avoided because it could spread cells.

Priority actions
  • Know which biopsy goes with which organ.
  • Remember the ovary is removed and examined rather than needle biopsied.
Patient example

A pelvic mass is suspected to be ovarian. The provider plans surgical removal and pathology instead of a needle biopsy.

Common trap

Do not assume every mass gets a needle biopsy.

Memory trick

Ovary = Operate, don't poke.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The endometrial biopsy is sensitive for high-grade cancer.
  • For a suspected ovarian mass a biopsy is .
  • A cervical biopsy is taken at .
Key ideas
  • Ovarian mass: biopsy is not recommended because it could spread cells; the diagnosis is surgical removal with pathology.
  • Uterine: endometrial biopsy is 99% sensitive for high-grade cancer; a D&C is done if the biopsy is negative but bleeding continues.
  • Cervical: colposcopy with biopsy after an abnormal Pap; the biopsy is diagnostic.
  • Lung: bronchoscopy views and biopsies the airways; mediastinoscopy is an incision to biopsy the mediastinum.
Source: study guide, Ch 13, Ch 26 and Ch 65

Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy

Mechanism first

The marrow is deep in the bone, so the needle goes in at a bony site with good access: the posterior iliac crest. Pain and bleeding follow from the needle and from low platelets.

Priority actions
  • Check consent, allergies, platelets and coagulation studies before.
  • Hold direct pressure and keep the dressing on afterward.
Patient example

A client with leukemia says the procedure might kill her. The nurse corrects the fear and explains pressure and a brief pulling pain.

Common trap

Do not choose supine for the posterior iliac crest.

Memory trick

Posterior = prone or side-lying.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The most common site is the .
  • Direct pressure is held for .
  • The dressing stays on at least .
Key ideas
  • The most common site is the posterior iliac crest with the client prone or side-lying; the sternum or anterior iliac crest is done supine.
  • Before: consent, allergies and bleeding risk. The client feels pressure and a brief pulling pain, and the procedure takes 5 to 10 minutes.
  • After: direct pressure for 5 to 10 minutes, a sterile dressing, rest for several hours, dressing on at least 24 hours.
  • Report bleeding that soaks the dressing or lasts more than 24 hours, and watch for infection.
Source: study guide, Ch 33

Lung cancer

Small cell versus non-small cell

Mechanism first

Smoking damages the lining of the airways, mutations pile up, and cells grow without dying. Small cell cancer is fast; non-small cell is slower.

Priority actions
  • Identify the cell type first because it decides treatment.
  • Teach smoking cessation and screening eligibility.
Patient example

A 68-year-old with a long smoking history has small cell cancer. Surgery is not the main treatment because it spreads early.

Common trap

Do not swap 15% and 85%, or give small cell the good early survival.

Memory trick

Small cell = Speedy, Spreads, Sad survival. NSCLC types = All Smokers Lose (Adeno, Squamous, Large).

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Small cell makes up of lung cancers.
  • More than of lung cancer is caused by smoking.
  • Non-small cell has a good 5-year survival if found .
Key ideas
  • Small cell is about 15%, grows fast and spreads early, has a poor outlook (class: 6 months to 1 year), and surgery is not the main treatment.
  • Non-small cell is about 85%, has three types (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large cell), is slower, and has a good 5-year survival if found early.
  • More than 90% of lung cancer is caused by smoking; yearly low-dose CT is for high-risk clients (20 pack-years, current smoker or quit within 15 years).
Source: study guide, Ch 26 and class notes

Lung cancer cues and diagnosis

Mechanism first

Early lung cancer is quiet; symptoms appear when the tumor irritates the airway, bleeds, blocks, or spreads.

Priority actions
  • Ask about cough change, hemoptysis, hoarseness, weight loss and bone pain.
  • Prepare for imaging, sputum and biopsy tests.
Patient example

A client with lung cancer reports a new headache and bone pain. The nurse suspects metastasis to the brain and bone.

Common trap

Do not call cough or hemoptysis a sign of spread; they are signs of the tumor in the lung.

Memory trick

PET = metabolism, CT = structure.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • A PET scan shows .
  • Headache and bone pain suggest .
  • Mediastinoscopy is a surgical incision to biopsy the .
Key ideas
  • Cues: new or changed cough, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, wheezing, hoarseness, chest pain, weight loss, frequent pneumonia.
  • Headache and bone pain suggest metastasis to brain and bone; common sites are brain, bone, adrenal gland and the other lung.
  • PET shows metabolic activity, not structure; sputum cytology, bronchoscopy and mediastinoscopy obtain cells or tissue.
Source: study guide, Ch 26

Lung cancer treatment

Mechanism first

Treatment matches how far the tumor has spread. Surgery removes it when it is localized; chemotherapy and radiation work when it is not.

Priority actions
  • Match the operation to the extent: wedge, lobectomy, pneumonectomy.
  • Dose pain medicine around the clock and start palliative care at diagnosis.
Patient example

A client with a tumor in one lobe and no metastasis is scheduled for a lobectomy.

Common trap

Do not think palliative care waits until the end of life.

Memory trick

Wedge < Lobe < Whole lung.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • A removes an entire lobe.
  • WHO step 3 uses a plus a nonopioid.
  • Palliative care begins at .
Key ideas
  • Lobectomy removes a lobe, pneumonectomy removes a lung, and a wedge resection removes a small section; surgery is preferred if there is no metastasis.
  • Chemotherapy is the primary treatment for advanced disease; radiation is used when surgery is not an option or for palliation.
  • WHO ladder: nonopioid, then moderate opioid plus nonopioid, then strong opioid plus nonopioid, given around the clock.
  • Palliative care begins at diagnosis.
Source: study guide, Ch 26

Lung cancer nursing care and chest tubes

Mechanism first

Tumor and surgery reduce the lung's ability to exchange gas. Position and oxygen help the lungs expand; the chest tube system needs a closed, open-draining path.

Priority actions
  • Give oxygen to keep SpO₂ at 90% or higher and raise the head to semi-Fowler's.
  • Keep the chest tube system closed and never clamp it.
Patient example

A client after lobectomy has constant bubbling in the water-seal chamber. That means an air leak in the system.

Common trap

Do not clamp the tube to stop a leak or to move the client.

Memory trick

Chest tube = never clamp, keep it closed.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Keep the SpO₂ at or higher.
  • Constant bubbling in the water seal means an .
  • A chest tube is clamped.
Key ideas
  • Give oxygen to keep the SpO₂ at 90% or higher and position the client in semi-Fowler's.
  • Small frequent meals with supplements; a large meal pushes on the diaphragm.
  • Never clamp a chest tube; keep the system closed; continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber is an air leak.
Source: study guide, Ch 26

Labs: CBC, WBC, platelets

CBC, WBC and ANC

Mechanism first

Marrow makes cells, and each count tells a story: red cells carry oxygen, white cells fight infection, platelets plug bleeding. Chemotherapy and leukemia change the counts.

Priority actions
  • Read the ANC for infection risk, not just the total WBC.
  • Use the correct tube: lavender for the CBC.
Patient example

A client on chemotherapy has an ANC of 400. The nurse starts neutropenic precautions and watches for fever.

Common trap

Do not read ANC as a platelet or red cell value.

Memory trick

NEB: Neutrophils, Eosinophils, Basophils are the granulocytes.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Neutropenia is an ANC below .
  • A left shift means many immature .
  • A CBC is drawn in a tube.
Key ideas
  • A CBC uses a lavender (EDTA) tube; PT, INR and PTT use sodium citrate.
  • A left shift is many immature neutrophils (bands) and means active infection.
  • Neutropenia is an ANC below 1,500; 500 or below needs neutropenic precautions.
  • Reticulocytes are immature RBCs: high means the marrow is responding, low means a hypoproliferative marrow.
  • Low MCV is microcytic (iron deficiency); high MCV is macrocytic (B12 or folate).
Source: study guide, Ch 33

Platelet thresholds

Mechanism first

Platelets plug holes. As the count falls, the risk of bleeding rises, which is why the thresholds trigger different actions.

Priority actions
  • Start bleeding precautions below 100,000.
  • Expect transfusion below 20,000.
Patient example

A client with platelets of 45,000 gets a soft toothbrush, an electric razor and no IM injections.

Common trap

Do not confuse bleeding precautions (platelets) with neutropenic precautions (ANC).

Memory trick

100 → 50 → 20 → 5: precautions, spontaneous, transfuse, fatal.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Bleeding precautions start below .
  • Platelets are usually transfused below .
  • A fatal CNS or GI bleed is possible below .
Key ideas
  • Normal platelets are 150,000 to 450,000/mm³.
  • Bleeding precautions start below 100,000; spontaneous bleeding is possible below 50,000.
  • Platelets are usually transfused below 20,000; below 5,000 a fatal CNS or GI bleed is possible.
Source: study guide, Ch 33 and Ch 34

Iron studies and the iron diet

Mechanism first

Iron builds hemoglobin. When stores run out, ferritin falls, transferrin has empty seats (high TIBC), and the cells are small and pale.

Priority actions
  • Hold iron supplements 24 hours before the test and draw in the morning.
  • Teach iron foods with vitamin C and no dairy.
Patient example

A client with iron deficiency anemia chooses roast beef, spinach, tomato soup and orange juice; that menu shows teaching worked.

Common trap

Do not pair iron with milk; dairy blocks absorption.

Memory trick

Ferritin = garage (stores), transferrin = bus, TIBC = empty seats.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • In iron deficiency TIBC is .
  • Hold iron supplements for before the test.
  • blocks iron absorption.
Key ideas
  • In iron deficiency ferritin and transferrin saturation are low, TIBC is high, and the cells are microcytic and hypochromic.
  • No iron supplements for 24 hours before a serum iron; draw it in the morning.
  • Eat heme iron (red meat) and nonheme iron (spinach, beans) with vitamin C; dairy blocks absorption.
Source: study guide, Ch 33 and Ch 34

Clotting studies

Mechanism first

Two clotting pathways join and each has a monitoring test and a drug that acts on it.

Priority actions
  • Use PTT for heparin and PT/INR for warfarin.
  • Know the INR goal of 2 to 3.
Patient example

A client on warfarin has an INR of 2.5, which is in range.

Common trap

If a question asks which lab monitors heparin, PTT is the safe answer.

Memory trick

PITT = PTT, Intrinsic, heparin. PET = PT, Extrinsic, warfarin.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Heparin is monitored with .
  • Warfarin is monitored with .
  • The INR goal on warfarin is .
Key ideas
  • The intrinsic pathway is monitored by PTT and heparin; the extrinsic pathway by PT/INR and warfarin.
  • The INR goal on warfarin is 2 to 3.
  • Bleeding time checks platelet function and is not done if platelets are under 75,000; platelet aggregation is impaired by aspirin, NSAIDs and von Willebrand disease.
Source: study guide, Ch 33

Leukemia: risk factors, medications

What leukemia does

Mechanism first

A mutated stem cell makes immature blasts that never mature or die. The marrow fills with them, so red cells and platelets fall and the blasts cannot fight infection.

Priority actions
  • Assess for anemia, bleeding and infection.
  • Recognize that a high WBC count can still mean infection risk.
Patient example

A child with the most common childhood leukemia has bruising and bone pain; ALL fits.

Common trap

A high count does not mean strong defense; the blasts do not work.

Memory trick

Acute = AML + ALL (sudden). Chronic = CML + CLL (years).

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The most common childhood leukemia is .
  • The crowded marrow causes anemia and .
  • CML and CLL are types.
Key ideas
  • A stem cell mutates into immature blasts that never mature or die, producing leukocytosis.
  • The crowded marrow cannot make enough RBCs and platelets, so anemia and thrombocytopenia occur.
  • The blasts cannot fight infection, so neutropenia and infection occur.
  • AML and ALL are acute and ALL is the most common childhood leukemia; CML and CLL are chronic and can turn acute.
Source: study guide, Ch 34

Leukemia risk factors

Mechanism first

Anything that damages marrow DNA raises risk: radiation, benzene, prior chemotherapy, smoking, or a chromosome problem such as Down syndrome.

Priority actions
  • Ask about occupation, prior chemotherapy and radiation.
  • Know the Philadelphia chromosome is the CML marker.
Patient example

A 62-year-old with decades at an oil refinery and Hgb 9.4 has benzene exposure, the highest risk in the case.

Common trap

Do not pick fatigue, bleeding gums or low Hgb as risk factors; they are effects.

Memory trick

Refinery = benzene = leukemia.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Down syndrome raises leukemia risk about .
  • The Philadelphia chromosome is found in more than of CML.
  • Oil refinery work means exposure.
Key ideas
  • Risk factors are genetic anomalies, Down syndrome, radiation, benzene or chemical exposure, prior chemotherapy or radiation, and smoking.
  • The Philadelphia chromosome (9;22) is found in more than 90% of CML.
  • Oil refinery work means benzene exposure, the highest risk factor in the case.
Source: study guide, Ch 34

Leukemia treatment and medications

Mechanism first

Chemotherapy kills the fast-dividing blasts in three phases, and each phase has a job.

Priority actions
  • Give chemotherapy as prescribed in phases.
  • Give prophylactic antimicrobials and blood products as ordered.
Patient example

A client in remission after induction still needs consolidation and maintenance because remission is not a cure.

Common trap

Do not tell a client in remission that she is cured.

Memory trick

I-C-M: Induce, Consolidate, Maintain.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Induction aims for .
  • Imatinib targets in CML.
  • Radiation reaches the CNS because chemotherapy cannot cross the .
Key ideas
  • Chemotherapy is given in phases: induction (get remission), consolidation (treat hidden disease), maintenance (prevent relapse); remission is not a cure.
  • AML induction example is daunorubicin plus cytarabine; imatinib targets Bcr-Abl in CML; ibrutinib is used in CLL.
  • Prophylactic antibiotics, antivirals and antifungals are given during neutropenia.
  • Radiation to the brain and spine treats CNS disease because chemotherapy cannot cross the blood–brain barrier.
  • The textbook says G-CSF (filgrastim) is generally not indicated in leukemia.
Source: study guide, Ch 34

Leukemia nursing priorities

Mechanism first

Few working neutrophils mean a fever may be the only sign of infection; low platelets mean bleeding. Both drive the nursing plan.

Priority actions
  • Treat fever as an emergency and call right away.
  • Teach bleeding and infection precautions and bank sperm or eggs.
Patient example

A client with ANC 0.6 and platelets 19,000 says she has a dental cleaning scheduled. She needs more teaching.

Common trap

Do not treat a fever with acetaminophen and wait.

Memory trick

Fever + low ANC = call now.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • After chemotherapy the first priority is .
  • Fever means broad-spectrum immediately.
  • No temperatures in neutropenia.
Key ideas
  • After chemotherapy the first priority is infection; fever means broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately.
  • Never take a rectal temperature in a neutropenic client.
  • Teach to avoid dental cleanings when platelets are low, and go to the ED for fever of 102°F, chills or a nosebleed over 10 minutes.
  • Offer sperm or egg banking before therapy.
Source: study guide, Ch 34

Neutropenic precautions

Neutropenia values and fever

Mechanism first

Neutrophils are the first cells to reach an infection. When the ANC drops, even small infections can spread fast.

Priority actions
  • Check the ANC on every chemotherapy client.
  • Start precautions at 500 or below.
Patient example

A client at home has a temperature of 100.6°F and should seek care right away.

Common trap

Do not wait to see if a fever settles.

Memory trick

1,500 = neutropenia, 500 = precautions, 100.4 = call.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Neutropenia is an ANC below .
  • Precautions start at an ANC of or below.
  • A temperature of or higher needs immediate care.
Key ideas
  • Neutropenia is an ANC below 1,500; precautions start at 500 or below.
  • A temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher needs immediate care and IV antibiotics.
  • Fever may be the first and only sign of infection.
Source: study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 34

Neutropenic precautions (Box 34.2)

Mechanism first

Every rule removes a source of germs: hands, sick people, plants and standing water, hard-to-wash fruit, and the rectal route.

Priority actions
  • Hand hygiene for everyone.
  • Remove plants and water sources; teach food safety and daily temperature checks.
Patient example

A client plans to put fresh cut flowers at the bedside; that statement needs correcting.

Common trap

Do not allow rectal temperatures, suppositories or enemas.

Memory trick

No flowers, no berries (rasp/black), no rectal.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Avoid .
  • Avoid .
  • Reverse isolation means staff wear .
Key ideas
  • Hand hygiene by everyone, a private room, avoid crowds, sick people, small children and pets.
  • No live plants or cut flowers, no standing water or humidifiers.
  • Wash raw fruits and vegetables well; avoid raspberries and blackberries.
  • No rectal temperatures, suppositories or enemas, because rectal bacteria can enter the blood.
  • Take prophylactic antimicrobials daily and finish the course; reverse isolation means staff wear PPE to protect the client.
Source: study guide, Ch 34 and class notes

Hodgkin lymphoma

Hodgkin lymphoma: signs and diagnosis

Mechanism first

A lymph node cell becomes a tumor and spreads along lymph tissue. Reed–Sternberg cells mark Hodgkin disease; B symptoms signal a heavier burden.

Priority actions
  • Assess nodes, B symptoms, skin from itching and breathing.
  • Prepare the client for a lymph node biopsy.
Patient example

A 24-year-old with painless neck swelling, drenching night sweats and itching has Reed–Sternberg cells on biopsy.

Common trap

Painful, tender nodes suggest infection, not lymphoma.

Memory trick

B symptoms: fever, drenching sweats, weight loss.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Hodgkin lymphoma is defined by cells.
  • A is definitive.
  • Generalized itching is common in lymphoma.
Key ideas
  • Reed–Sternberg cells define Hodgkin lymphoma; it has a better survival rate than non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
  • Painless lymph node swelling; B symptoms are low-grade fever, drenching night sweats and weight loss.
  • Itching is common in Hodgkin lymphoma; a dry cough worse lying flat suggests a mediastinal mass.
  • A lymph node biopsy is definitive; uric acid and LDH are elevated.
Source: study guide, Ch 34

Lymphoma complications and nursing

Mechanism first

A growing node mass compresses nearby structures: the vena cava, the spinal cord; bone involvement raises calcium.

Priority actions
  • Recognize the three emergencies and call at once.
  • Teach neutropenic and bleeding precautions before chemotherapy.
Patient example

A client with facial and arm swelling, dyspnea and trouble swallowing has superior vena cava syndrome.

Common trap

Do not mix SVC syndrome with tumor lysis, SIADH or bowel obstruction.

Memory trick

SVC = swelling above the chest. Cord = back pain then numbness. Calcium = polyuria, confusion.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Hypercalcemia is a calcium above .
  • Lymphoma stage II is nodes on the of the diaphragm.
  • Stage IV is .
Key ideas
  • Superior vena cava syndrome: facial and arm swelling, dyspnea, chest pain, dysphagia.
  • Spinal cord compression: back pain, then sensory and motor change; an emergency.
  • Hypercalcemia above 11 mg/dL: confusion, polyuria, heart block; IV fluids dilute calcium.
  • Lymphoma staging: I one node, II two or more nodes on one side of the diaphragm, III both sides, IV organs plus nodes.
  • Teach neutropenic and bleeding precautions before chemotherapy.
Source: study guide, Ch 34

Multiple myeloma

Myeloma: patho and CRAB

Mechanism first

One clone of plasma cells overgrows the marrow and releases M protein. Bone is eaten away (calcium rises) and light chains injure the kidney.

Priority actions
  • Look for CRAB.
  • Protect the kidneys.
Patient example

A client with back pain, calcium 12, creatinine 2.4 and Hgb 9 meets three CRAB criteria.

Common trap

Do not confuse myeloma with leukemia or Hodgkin lymphoma markers.

Memory trick

CRAB = Calcium, Renal, Anemia, Bone.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Hypercalcemia in CRAB is above .
  • Bence Jones protein is in the urine.
  • Myeloma is a cancer of cells.
Key ideas
  • A clone of plasma cells makes an M protein; lytic bone lesions release calcium.
  • CRAB: hypercalcemia above 11.5, renal insufficiency (creatinine above 2), anemia (Hgb below 10), bone disease.
  • Excess light chains (Bence Jones protein) are toxic to the kidneys.
  • Myeloma is an incurable B-cell cancer of plasma cells.
Source: study guide, Ch 34

Myeloma nursing interventions

Mechanism first

Bone breakdown releases calcium, which injures the kidney and weakens bone. Fluids, movement and bone-protecting drugs address each.

Priority actions
  • Push fluids, ambulate as tolerated, and monitor calcium, BUN and creatinine.
  • Report sudden severe pain or new numbness at once.
Patient example

A client with myeloma reports sudden severe back pain and leg numbness. The nurse assesses and reports for possible fracture or cord compression.

Common trap

Do not give calcium or restrict fluids.

Memory trick

Fluids, Feet (walk), bisphosphonate.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Encourage to dilute calcium.
  • Bisphosphonates reduce .
  • Thalidomide and lenalidomide are .
Key ideas
  • Encourage fluids to dilute calcium and protect the kidneys; monitor serum and urine calcium, BUN and creatinine.
  • Encourage ambulation as tolerated and position for comfort.
  • Bisphosphonates such as ibandronate (Boniva) reduce bone breakdown, which lowers calcium and fractures.
  • Sudden severe pain or new numbness may mean a fracture or cord compression: report at once.
  • Thalidomide and lenalidomide are teratogenic.
Source: study guide, Ch 34 and class notes

Breast cancer (female and male): medications

Breast cancer treatment

Mechanism first

Breast tumors are removed (lumpectomy or mastectomy) and the remaining cells are treated with radiation, chemotherapy and hormones.

Priority actions
  • Know the order: surgery, chemotherapy, then radiation.
  • Know which lesions need treatment.
Patient example

A client plans chemotherapy first, then mastectomy, then oral hormone therapy; the chemotherapy is neoadjuvant and the hormone therapy adjuvant.

Common trap

Do not skip radiation after lumpectomy.

Memory trick

Neo = New = first; adjuvant = after.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Lumpectomy is always followed by .
  • DCIS .
  • LCIS has and is followed with mammograms.
Key ideas
  • Lumpectomy is always followed by radiation; with chemotherapy the order is surgery, chemotherapy, then radiation.
  • Neoadjuvant therapy is given before the primary treatment; adjuvant therapy is given after.
  • DCIS is stage 0 and requires surgery; LCIS has no treatment and is followed with mammograms.
Source: study guide, Ch 65

Breast cancer medications (Table 65.3)

Mechanism first

Hormone drugs starve estrogen-fed tumors in two ways, and targeted drugs attack HER2.

Priority actions
  • Question oral contraceptives in estrogen-positive disease.
  • Teach side effects and the SSRI interaction.
Patient example

A client on tamoxifen starts an SSRI; the nurse reports it because SSRIs reduce tamoxifen metabolism.

Common trap

Do not give aromatase inhibitors the tamoxifen warnings or vice versa.

Memory trick

Tamoxifen = Blocks the receptor; AIs = Stop the making; Trastuzumab = HER2 and heart.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Tamoxifen blocks estrogen at its .
  • Aromatase inhibitors risk .
  • Trastuzumab can cause .
Key ideas
  • Tamoxifen blocks estrogen at its receptor for 5 to 10 years; avoid SSRIs and question oral contraceptives in estrogen-positive disease.
  • Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) stop androgens becoming estrogen; they risk osteoporosis and fractures.
  • Trastuzumab is for HER2-positive tumors and can cause cardiotoxicity; pembrolizumab is immunotherapy with rash, diarrhea and thyroid problems.
Source: study guide, Ch 65 and Davis Table 65.3

Male breast cancer

Mechanism first

Men have little breast tissue, so tumors reach the nipple, skin and muscle quickly; BRCA2 is the usual gene.

Priority actions
  • Check receptor status before hormone therapy.
  • Use ultrasound under 25 and mammogram at 25 or older.
Patient example

A man with receptor-negative disease after mastectomy has an antiestrogen order; the nurse questions it.

Common trap

Do not choose lumpectomy because the tissue is small.

Memory trick

Few cells, fast spread, mastectomy.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Male breast cancer is about less common than in women.
  • The more common mutation is .
  • Hormone therapy is only for tumors.
Key ideas
  • It is about 100 times less common than in women, occurs at ages 60 to 70, and BRCA2 is the more common mutation.
  • With little breast tissue it spreads early to the nipple, skin and muscle; mastectomy is usual.
  • Hormone therapy is only for receptor-positive tumors, so question antiestrogen therapy in a receptor-negative client.
  • Ultrasound is used under age 25; mammogram at 25 or older.
Source: study guide, Ch 66

Breast cancer nursing care

Mechanism first

Surgery, node removal and radiation each leave a typical complication.

Priority actions
  • Watch the drainage and the incision.
  • Teach arm care, shoulder exercises and skin care.
Patient example

A client after mastectomy has bloody drainage saturating the dressing; she needs immediate attention.

Common trap

Do not teach monthly breast self-exam as the recommended screening.

Memory trick

Node out, arm up (lymphedema); frozen shoulder is the common long-term effect.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Arm swelling after node removal is .
  • Radiation can cause weeks to months later.
  • Breast self-exam is .
Key ideas
  • Bloody drainage saturating the dressing is the most concerning wound finding; serosanguineous drainage is expected.
  • Lymphedema follows axillary node removal; shoulder immobility is the most common long-term effect.
  • Radiation effects: skin redness, itching, desquamation, breast swelling, and pneumonitis 6 weeks to 6 months later.
  • Breast self-exam is not recommended; screening is by mammography.
Source: study guide, Ch 65

Uterine cancer

Uterine cancer risk

Mechanism first

Estrogen without progesterone makes the uterine lining keep growing. Fat tissue makes estrogen, so obesity adds to the effect.

Priority actions
  • Teach that estrogen therapy with a uterus needs progesterone.
  • Watch tamoxifen users.
Patient example

A 52-year-old with a uterus starts estrogen; the nurse explains the need for progesterone.

Common trap

Do not blame HPV; that is cervical.

Memory trick

Estrogen alone = unopposed = uterine risk.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The number one risk factors are unopposed estrogen and .
  • About are endometrioid adenocarcinoma.
  • Usual age is .
Key ideas
  • The most common gynecologic cancer in the US, usually at ages 55 to 65.
  • The number one risk factors are unopposed estrogen and obesity; tamoxifen, early menarche, late menopause, PCOS and diabetes add risk.
  • About 80% are endometrioid adenocarcinoma; anyone on estrogen with a uterus needs progesterone.
Source: study guide, Ch 65 and Ch 13

Uterine cancer diagnosis and treatment

Mechanism first

A thick or abnormal lining bleeds; so bleeding is the sign and a biopsy of the lining is the test.

Priority actions
  • Treat any postmenopausal bleeding as a reason to evaluate.
  • Teach comfort measures during chemotherapy.
Patient example

A 60-year-old who calls about vaginal bleeding needs follow-up first.

Common trap

Do not choose CA-125 or colposcopy; those belong to ovarian and cervical cancer.

Memory trick

Bleeding = biopsy of the lining.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The most common symptom is abnormal .
  • First test: .
  • Treatment removes the uterus, tubes and .
Key ideas
  • Abnormal uterine or postmenopausal bleeding is the most common symptom and needs evaluation.
  • Endometrial biopsy first; ultrasound shows a thickened endometrium; D&C if the biopsy is negative but bleeding continues.
  • Treatment is removal of the uterus, tubes and ovaries; radiation is the usual adjuvant.
  • Stomatitis: salt-water rinses and avoid hot or spicy food.
Source: study guide, Ch 65

Cervical guidelines

Cervical screening guidelines

Mechanism first

Cervical cells change slowly, so screening on a schedule finds the change before it becomes cancer.

Priority actions
  • Count the age first, then pick the test and interval.
  • Know when HPV testing is allowed.
Patient example

A 25-year-old with a normal Pap at 21 and no primary HPV available gets breast exam, pelvic exam and a Pap (no HPV cotest before 30).

Common trap

Do not start screening at first intercourse or before 21.

Memory trick

21 Pap/3, 25 HPV/5, 30 any of three.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The first Pap is at age .
  • Pap alone is repeated every .
  • Primary HPV is repeated every .
Key ideas
  • No screening before age 21; the first Pap is at 21 and is repeated every 3 years until 29.
  • HPV testing is not a screen at 21 to 29, except as a reflex if atypical cells are found; primary HPV may start at 25 every 5 years.
  • Ages 30 to 65: primary HPV or Pap plus HPV cotest every 5 years, or Pap alone every 3 years.
  • Screening may stop after 65 with adequate negative results and no CIN 2 in 20 years.
Source: study guide, Ch 65 and class PLQ

Cervical cancer cause, signs and work-up

Mechanism first

HPV changes cervical cells in the transformation zone; early change has no symptoms, so only screening finds it.

Priority actions
  • Refer abnormal results for colposcopy and biopsy.
  • Teach vaccination and screening.
Patient example

A client with a high-risk HPV test and abnormal Pap goes for colposcopy with biopsy.

Common trap

Do not tell a client the HPV vaccine treats an infection.

Memory trick

Dysplasia is silent; bleeding after sex is the late warning.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The cause of cervical cancer is .
  • Vaginal bleeding, especially after , is the most common symptom.
  • Nothing in the vagina for before colposcopy.
Key ideas
  • HPV is the cause; the HPV vaccine at age 11 to 12 (as early as 9) does not treat an existing infection.
  • Dysplasia has no symptoms; vaginal bleeding, especially after intercourse, is the most common symptom of invasive cancer.
  • An abnormal Pap with high-risk HPV leads to colposcopy with biopsy; nothing in the vagina for 24 hours before, and Lugol's is contraindicated with iodine or shellfish allergy.
  • About 90% are squamous cell carcinomas in the transformation zone.
Source: study guide, Ch 65 and Ch 64

Cervical cancer treatment

Mechanism first

Treatment depends on how far the cancer has spread and on whether fertility matters.

Priority actions
  • Offer fertility options for early disease.
  • Use chemoradiation for higher stages.
Patient example

A 29-year-old wanting children with early disease is offered a radical trachelectomy.

Common trap

Do not offer exenteration for early disease; it is for pelvic recurrence.

Memory trick

Keep fertility: trachelectomy. No fertility wish: hysterectomy.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • A radical trachelectomy removes the only.
  • Higher stages use .
  • Pelvic exenteration treats a .
Key ideas
  • Early disease: cone biopsy or radical trachelectomy if fertility is wanted; hysterectomy with node dissection if not.
  • Higher stages: chemoradiation with brachytherapy.
  • Pelvic exenteration can cure a recurrence confined to the pelvis.
Source: study guide, Ch 65

Prostate cancer: post-op complications

Prostate cancer patho and screening

Mechanism first

The tumor grows in the outer part of the gland, away from the urethra, so it is silent until it spreads. PSA rises with several conditions, so biopsy decides.

Priority actions
  • Use PSA of 4 or higher as a trigger for work-up.
  • Confirm with biopsy.
Patient example

A man with bone metastases says he never had urinary trouble; the tumor grew on the periphery.

Common trap

PSA does not confirm cancer and cannot separate it from BPH.

Memory trick

Edge growth = silent; PSA = signal, biopsy = proof.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Tumors grow on the of the gland.
  • A PSA of or higher needs evaluation.
  • African American men have the mortality.
Key ideas
  • Tumors grow on the periphery of the gland, so urinary symptoms come late; spread is to lymph nodes, bone, rectum and bladder.
  • PSA of 4 ng/mL or higher needs further assessment; PSA has high sensitivity but low specificity and cannot tell BPH from cancer.
  • A needle biopsy confirms the diagnosis, followed by a Gleason score.
  • African American men have a higher incidence and twice the mortality; BPH is not a precursor to prostate cancer.
Source: study guide, Ch 66

Prostate cancer treatment and safety

Mechanism first

Radioactive seeds irradiate the tumor from inside; hormone therapy removes the testosterone that feeds it.

Priority actions
  • Teach brachytherapy safety.
  • Limit contact and use thicker PPE.
Patient example

A client with seeds is told to avoid sex for 2 weeks and then use a condom.

Common trap

External beam clients are not radioactive; brachytherapy clients are handled with caution.

Memory trick

Seeds in = PPE on.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Brachytherapy seeds are placed through the .
  • No sex for , then a condom.
  • Chemotherapy is used when the cancer is .
Key ideas
  • Brachytherapy seeds are placed permanently through the perineum for cancer confined to the prostate; no sex for 2 weeks, then use a condom.
  • The nurse minimizes contact and wears proper, thicker PPE with brachytherapy; an external beam client is not radioactive.
  • Ablative hormone therapy suppresses testosterone; chemotherapy is for hormone-refractory disease.
Source: study guide, Ch 66 and class notes

Post-op complications after prostatectomy

Mechanism first

Surgery cuts nerves, muscle and vessels around the prostate: erections, urine control and bleeding are affected, and wounds can become infected.

Priority actions
  • Manage bladder irrigation, stool softeners and aseptic wound care.
  • Teach what to report.
Patient example

A client with a fever, malaise and a high WBC after treatment most likely has an infection.

Common trap

Do not assume nerve-sparing surgery guarantees erections.

Memory trick

I-I-I-B: Impotence, Incontinence, Infection, Bleeding.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The most expected complication is .
  • Bladder irrigation clears .
  • Stool softeners prevent .
Key ideas
  • Impotence is the most expected; nerve-sparing surgery only tries to protect the erection nerves.
  • Watch for urinary incontinence, infection (fever, pain, swelling, redness) and bleeding with clots.
  • Manage bladder irrigation to clear clots and give stool softeners to avoid straining.
  • A cancer client with fever, malaise and high WBC most likely has an infection.
Source: study guide, Ch 66 and class PLQ

Testicular cancer

Testicular cancer risk, signs and markers

Mechanism first

An undescended testicle is the strongest risk; the tumor forms a painless mass and releases markers that can be measured.

Priority actions
  • Teach self-exam in a warm shower.
  • Know the markers AFP and hCG.
Patient example

A 31-year-old with a painless heavy scrotal mass and a childhood undescended testicle likely has testicular cancer.

Common trap

Do not expect pain; painful scrotum suggests infection or injury.

Memory trick

Cryptorchid, painless, AFP + hCG.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • The greatest risk factor is .
  • The classic sign is a mass.
  • AFP and hCG should after removal.
Key ideas
  • Cryptorchidism is the greatest risk factor; the average age is 33.
  • The classic sign is a painless mass, sometimes with a firm or heavy feeling.
  • AFP and hCG should fall after the tumor is removed; if not, look for more tumor.
  • Cure rate is 90 to 100% if found early.
Source: study guide, Ch 66

Testicular cancer treatment and teaching

Mechanism first

Removing the testicle removes the tumor and gives the diagnosis; additional treatment depends on the cell type.

Priority actions
  • Bank sperm first.
  • Teach follow-up for at least 10 years.
Patient example

A client with nonseminoma gets surgery, node removal and chemotherapy, not radiation.

Common trap

Do not give nonseminoma radiation; it is not responsive.

Memory trick

Seminoma = Sensitive to radiation.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • All types start with .
  • Follow-up lasts at least .
  • Bleomycin can damage the .
Key ideas
  • All types start with removal of the affected testicle (orchiectomy).
  • Seminoma is radiation sensitive; nonseminoma is not and gets node removal and chemotherapy.
  • Bank sperm before treatment; follow up for at least 10 years; retroperitoneal node removal can damage ejaculation nerves.
  • Bleomycin can damage the lungs and ifosfamide can cause hemorrhagic cystitis.
  • After surgery, hypotension with tachycardia means volume loss and fever means infection.
Source: study guide, Ch 66

End of life: hospice vs palliative

Hospice versus palliative care

Mechanism first

Palliative care treats symptoms and can run alongside cure-directed care. Hospice replaces cure-directed care with comfort when time is short.

Priority actions
  • Start palliative care at diagnosis.
  • Offer hospice when the prognosis is 6 months or less and the client chooses comfort.
Patient example

A client with heart failure who still wants every treatment is a palliative care client, not hospice.

Common trap

Do not say palliative means end of life.

Memory trick

Palliative = Parallel to treatment. Hospice = Home stretch.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Hospice is for a prognosis of .
  • Palliative care can continue with treatment.
  • All hospice is .
Key ideas
  • Palliative care is for any stage of serious illness, begins at diagnosis, and can continue with curative treatment.
  • Hospice is for a prognosis of 6 months or less; curative treatment stops and the goal is comfort.
  • All hospice is palliative, but not all palliative care is hospice.
Source: study guide, Ch 26 and Other Topics

Nursing care at the end of life

Mechanism first

As the body shuts down, intake, urine output and circulation fall and breathing changes.

Priority actions
  • Medicate for pain and dyspnea on schedule.
  • Provide mouth care, repositioning and emotional and spiritual support.
Patient example

A hospice client has noisy secretions and mottled extremities; the nurse continues comfort care and talks to the client.

Common trap

Do not withhold opioids for fear of breathing changes.

Memory trick

Cold, mottled, noisy: comfort, comfort, comfort.

Tap to reveal the blanks
  • Hearing is often the sense lost.
  • Extremities become .
  • Honor the advance directive and order.
Key ideas
  • Signs death is near: falling intake and urine output, mottled cool extremities, apnea periods, noisy secretions.
  • Give opioids around the clock for pain and dyspnea, provide mouth care and repositioning, and honor advance directives.
  • Hearing is often the last sense lost.
Source: study guide, Other Topics

Read me

The same page is in the drill and in the Mastery Study Guide. They are built from the same facts and always agree.

How to use the drill

  1. Start with the pre-test. It asks a few questions from every topic (none from the last pass) and shows your level in each: Strong, Okay or Weak.
  2. Do your daily sessions. Pick topics, a length (5 to 500, endless, or a timed 30 or 45 minute plan) and tap Start. Leave Think first on: try to recall the answer before the choices appear.
  3. Check each answer. Read “Why my pick is wrong”, then the key idea. After a right answer tap Knew it or I guessed. A guess comes back sooner.
  4. Star anything you want to see again. Use the filters (missed, starred, last pass, never practiced) to drill just those.
  5. Fix my misses shows the mistakes you keep making and your shaky questions by concept. “Fix this” re-teaches the concept and asks you a different question on it.
  6. Last pass. Use it in the final days. It asks every last-pass question once, shakiest first. “Just the 20 weakest” is the short version.
  7. A question is solid only after you get the whole question right on two spaced visits (three for true/false). Your progress is saved on this device and, when you open the page as a claude.ai artifact, in your account so your phone and laptop match.

How to use the guide

  1. The guide teaches the same facts in lecture order. Each section gives the mechanism first, then the priority actions, a patient example, the common trap and a memory trick.
  2. Tap each blank to reveal it, but say the answer out loud first.
  3. The Key ideas box at the end of each section is the short version to re-read the night before.

How to use both together

  • Drill to find and prove. The drill finds what you do not know yet and proves what you do.
  • Guide to look up and re-learn. When a card in Fix my misses shows a concept, tap its link to open the same section in the guide. Read that section, then go back and prove it in the drill.
  • Every fact on a Fix my misses card is in the guide section it links to.
